query: Which material can be used for improve the magnetocaloric properties, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a portion of non‐magnetic refractory elements in a high‐entropy alloy (such as NbMoTaW) with ferromagnetic ones (e.g., Fe or Co) and processing the alloy by rapid solidification (selective laser melting) to obtain a fine‐grained microstructure will improve its magnetocaloric properties relative to conventional magnetocaloric materials.
generation.material_initial_state: A BCC-structured NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy produced via selective laser melting, noted for its fine microstructure (grain sizes ~13 μm) and mechanical robustness.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by partially replacing one or more of the refractory, non‐magnetic elements (e.g., substituting a fraction of Nb or Mo) with ferromagnetic elements such as Fe or Co, and process the modified alloy under similar selective laser melting conditions.
generation.conditions: Under cyclic magnetic fields near ambient or application-relevant temperatures where magnetocaloric effects are typically measured.
generation.structural_mediator: The refined, fine-grained microstructure induced by rapid solidification (via SLM) that can help in creating uniform magnetic domains and possibly improved magnetic exchange interactions in the doped alloy.
generation.mechanism: Introducing ferromagnetic elements is expected to yield a composition that undergoes a magnetic phase transition, while the fine microstructure from SLM helps in achieving uniform magnetic domain structures. Together, these factors can result in an enhanced magnetic entropy change when the material is exposed to varying magnetic fields.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified high-entropy alloy should exhibit a larger magnetization change and a greater adiabatic temperature change (i.e., larger magnetocaloric effect) than its undoped counterpart or conventional refractory alloys.
generation.baseline: Conventional magnetocaloric materials such as Gd-based alloys, whose magnetocaloric effect has been well characterized.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated only if the ferromagnetic substitution does not compromise structural stability and if the microstructure remains fine and homogeneous; the effect’s magnitude is unknown without targeted magnetic characterization.
generation.uncertainty: There is considerable uncertainty because the eligible evidence focuses on microstructural and mechanical improvements in a refractory HEA (NbMoTaW) without any direct magnetocaloric measurements, and the effect of ferromagnetic doping on magnetocaloric performance in such systems has not been established.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: (1) the base refractory HEA (NbMoTaW) processed via SLM, and (2) a doped version where a predetermined fraction of one non-magnetic element is replaced with a ferromagnetic element (e.g., Fe or Co). Process both sets using identical selective laser melting parameters. Subject both materials to cyclic magnetic fields over a range of temperatures while measuring their magnetization, and determine the adiabatic temperature change using standard magnetocaloric effect measurement methods.
measurements: Magnetization versus temperature (M-T curves) under applied magnetic fields
Magnetic entropy change (ΔS_m) via magnetization measurements
Adiabatic temperature change (ΔT_ad) under magnetic field cycling
Microstructural analysis (grain size, phase purity) using SEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant enhancement in magnetic entropy change and adiabatic temperature change compared to the undoped alloy or falls short of established benchmarks for magnetocaloric materials (e.g., Gd-based alloys), then the hypothesis that the introduced ferromagnetic element and fine microstructure improve the magnetocaloric effect must be rejected.

Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite processing challenges, and how do its microstructure, hardness, and corrosion resistance compare to traditional superalloys and arc-melted counterparts?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition of Nb, Mo, Ta, W powders with 99.9% purity). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); parameters included hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, and a triple-pass remelting strategy (3x energy input) to achieve a linear energy density of 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance evaluated via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning range −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V).
